claim: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune rheumatic disease characterized by the presence of circulating autoantibodies against nuclear antigens.
source: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune rheumatic disease, characterized by the presence of circulating autoantibodies against nuclear antigens.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SLE from the medical literature, supported by citations to Dall'Era, 2013 and Petri et al., 2012.

claim: Clinical manifestations of SLE vary among affected individuals and can involve many organs and systems including the skin, joints, kidneys, heart, lungs, nervous system, and hematopoietic system.
source: Clinical manifestations vary among affected individuals and can involve many organs and systems, including the skin, joints, kidneys, heart, lungs, nervous system, and hematopoietic system (Dall'Era, 2013; Petri et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SLE clinical presentation, supported by citations.

claim: The prevalence of SLE ranges from 0.4 to 2 per 1000 individuals.
source: The prevalence of SLE ranges from 0.4 to 2/1000, varying with sex, age, and ancestry, and is more common in women of childbearing age and individuals of African, Asian, and Hispanic ancestry (Dall'Era, 2013; Petri et al., 2012; Rees et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 1995; Feldman et al., 2013; Somers et al., 2014; Lim et al., 2014; Ferucci et al., 2014; Chakravarty et al., 2007).
evidence: This prevalence data is supported by multiple epidemiological studies cited.

claim: SLE is more common in women of childbearing age and individuals of African, Asian, and Hispanic ancestry.
source: The prevalence of SLE ranges from 0.4 to 2/1000, varying with sex, age, and ancestry, and is more common in women of childbearing age and individuals of African, Asian, and Hispanic ancestry (Dall'Era, 2013; Petri et al., 2012; Rees et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 1995; Feldman et al., 2013; Somers et al., 2014; Lim et al., 2014; Ferucci et al., 2014; Chakravarty et al., 2007).
evidence: This demographic pattern is supported by multiple epidemiological studies.

claim: Sex, hormones, and environmental factors including drugs, chemical exposures, viral infections, and sunlight contribute to SLE disease.
source: Sex, hormones, and environmental factors, including drugs and chemical exposures, viral infections, and sunlight, contribute to the disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SLE risk factors.

claim: Specific therapies for SLE are currently limited.
source: Currently, specific therapies for SLE are limited (Hoi and Morand, 2021)
evidence: This statement about therapeutic limitations is supported by a citation.

claim: Lupus nephritis is one of the most common and serious manifestations of SLE and remains a major risk factor for morbidity and mortality.
source: clinical manifestations such as lupus nephritis, one of the most common and serious manifestations of SLE, remain a major risk factor for morbidity and mortality (Tektonidou et al., 2016; Menez et al., 2018; Hanly et al., 2016; Parikh et al., 2020).
evidence: This clinical characterization is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The contribution of genetics to SLE is supported by familial aggregation.
source: The contribution of genetics to SLE is supported by epidemiological data showing familial aggregation (Arnett and Shulman, 1976; Alarcón-Segovia et al., 2005; Reichlin et al., 1992)
evidence: This genetic contribution is supported by epidemiological studies cited.

claim: Monozygotic twins have higher concordance rates for SLE than dizygotic twins.
source: higher concordance rates between monozygotic than dizygotic twins (Deapen et al., 1992)
evidence: This twin study data is supported by citation.

claim: Autosomal recessive deficiency in PKCdelta or DNAse1L3 is associated with familial SLE.
source: the association of autosomal recessive deficiency in PKCdelta or DNAse1L3 with familial SLE, and similar phenotypes in the corresponding mouse models (Belot et al., 2013; Kiykim et al., 2015; Salzer et al., 2013; Al Mayouf et al., 2011; Ozçakar et al., 2013; Sisirak et al., 2016).
evidence: This genetic association is supported by multiple citations including mouse model data.

claim: Genome wide association studies in large populations of patients have implicated a number of genes associated with immune system function in SLE.
source: In addition, genome wide association studies in large populations of patients have implicated a number of genes associated with immune system function (Dall'Era, 2013; Teruel and Alarcón-Riquelme, 2016)
evidence: This GWAS finding is supported by citations.

claim: An SLE-like disease is observed in a proportion of patients with immunodeficiency due to autosomal recessive or X-linked C1q, C1r/s, C2, C4, and NADPH-Oxidase deficiencies.
source: an SLE-like disease is observed in a proportion of patients with immunodeficiency due to autosomal recessive or X-linked C1q, C1r/s, C2, C4, and NADPH-Oxidase deficiencies (Pickering et al., 2000; Winkelstein et al., 2000; Foster et al., 1998; van den Berg et al., 2009; Ling et al., 2018)
evidence: This association with complement and NADPH-oxidase deficiencies is supported by multiple citations.

claim: SLE-like disease is observed in patients with Rasopathies due to autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutations in the RAS pathway.
source: with Rasopathies due to autosomal dominant gain-of-function mutations in the RAS pathway (Bader-Meunier et al., 2013)
evidence: This association with Rasopathies is supported by citation.

claim: SLE-like disease is observed in a proportion of patients presenting with interferonopathies with bi-allelic or mono-allelic mutations in genes coding for nucleic acid sensors such as TREX1, STING, SAMHD1, ADAR, and IFIH1.
source: a proportion of patients presenting with interferonopathies with bi-allelic or mono-allelic mutations in genes coding for nucleic acid sensors such as TREX1, STING, SAMHD1, ADAR, and IFIH1 (Jeremiah et al., 2014; Crow et al., 2015; Lee-Kirsch et al., 2007; Ramantani et al., 2011).
evidence: This association with interferonopathies is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The study performed a forward genetic screen in multiplex SLE families with lupus nephritis to identify new SLE causing genes and molecular pathways.
source: In this study, we performed a forward genetic screen in multiplex SLE families with a well-defined phenotype, lupus nephritis, to identify new SLE causing genes and molecular pathways involved in SLE.
evidence: This describes the study design and approach.

claim: The study identified novel and rare deleterious variant alleles of TNK2/ACK1 and PTK6/BRK in two multiplex families.
source: We report the characterization of novel and rare deleterious variant alleles of two genes encoding the NRTK tyrosine kinase non-receptor 2/activated CDC42 kinase 1 (TNK2/ACK1) and protein tyrosine kinase 6/breast tumor kinase (PTK6/BRK) in two multiplex families.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic screen.

claim: The ACK1 and BRK variant alleles strongly decrease ACK1 and BRK kinase activity.
source: The variant alleles strongly decrease ACK1 and BRK kinase activity.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: ACK1 and BRK control B-cell and T-cell proliferation, survival, and activation.
source: ACK1 and BRK were shown to control B-cell and T-cell proliferation, survival, and activation (Kasprzycka et al., 2006; Sridaran et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ACK1 and BRK genetic deficiency or pharmacological inhibition does not result in spontaneous lupus development in C57BL/6 mice.
source: Although ACK1- and BRK- genetic deficiency (Sridaran et al., 2022; Haegebarth et al., 2006) or their pharmacological inhibition does not result in spontaneous lupus development in C57BL/6 mice
evidence: This is supported by citations and the study's own observations.

claim: ACK1 or BRK inhibitors aggravate IgG glomerular deposition in the kidneys of BALB/cByJ mice treated with pristane.
source: we show that ACK1 or BRK inhibitors aggravate IgG glomerular deposition in the kidneys of BALB/cByJ mice treated with pristane to induce a lupus-like disease (Satoh and Reeves, 1994)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the mouse studies.

claim: ACK1 or BRK inhibitors increase serum autoantibody levels in pristane-treated BALB/cByJ mice.
source: we show that ACK1 or BRK inhibitors aggravate IgG glomerular deposition in the kidneys of BALB/cByJ mice treated with pristane to induce a lupus-like disease (Satoh and Reeves, 1994) and increases serum autoantibody levels.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the mouse studies.

claim: NRTKs mediate phosphorylation of downstream effectors including RAC1, AKT, and STAT1/3, which are involved in immune cell homeostasis.
source: NRTKs mediate phosphorylation of downstream effectors, including RAC1, AKT, and STAT1/3, which are involved in immune cells homeostasis, and their deficiency can cause autoimmunity through different mechanisms (Yu et al., 2001.)
evidence: This is established knowledge about NRTK signaling supported by citation.

claim: NRTK deficiency can cause autoimmunity through different mechanisms.
source: NRTKs mediate phosphorylation of downstream effectors, including RAC1, AKT, and STAT1/3, which are involved in immune cells homeostasis, and their deficiency can cause autoimmunity through different mechanisms (Yu et al., 2001.)
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: NRTKs such as ACK1, Src, and PTK2/FAK are targets of MERTK.
source: NRTKs such as ACK1 (Mahajan et al., 2005), Src (Yi et al., 2009), and PTK2/FAK (Wu et al., 2005; Tibrewal et al., 2008) are also targets of MERTK
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: MERTK mediates efferocytosis, the recognition of phosphatidylserine on apoptotic cells for their anti-inflammatory engulfment.
source: MERTK, which mediates efferocytosis, the recognition of phosphatidylserine (PtdSer) on apoptotic cells for their anti-inflammatory engulfment (Wanke et al., 2021; Scott et al., 2001; Seitz et al., 2007; Cohen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MERTK function supported by citations.

claim: MERTK deficiency is a cause of SLE-like disease.
source: MERTK deficiency is a cause of SLE-like disease (Cohen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The patients' ACK1 and BRK variants are kinase dead in response to MERTK activation.
source: We found that the patients' ACK1 and BRK variants are kinase dead in response to MERTK activation and fail to phosphorylate AKT and STAT3, and to activate RAC1.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from biochemical assays.

claim: The patients' ACK1 and BRK variants fail to phosphorylate AKT and STAT3.
source: We found that the patients' ACK1 and BRK variants are kinase dead in response to MERTK activation and fail to phosphorylate AKT and STAT3, and to activate RAC1.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from biochemical assays.

claim: The patients' ACK1 and BRK variants fail to activate RAC1.
source: We found that the patients' ACK1 and BRK variants are kinase dead in response to MERTK activation and fail to phosphorylate AKT and STAT3, and to activate RAC1.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from biochemical assays.

claim: Human iPSC-derived macrophages from patients and isogenic variants presented with defective AKT/STAT3-driven anti-inflammatory response in response to apoptotic cells.
source: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived macrophages from patients and isogenic variants presented with defective AKT/STAT3-driven anti-inflammatory response and control of TNF and IL1β production in response to apoptotic cells
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from iPSC-derived macrophage studies.

claim: Human iPSC-derived macrophages from patients and isogenic variants had defective control of TNF and IL1β production in response to apoptotic cells.
source: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived macrophages from patients and isogenic variants presented with defective AKT/STAT3-driven anti-inflammatory response and control of TNF and IL1β production in response to apoptotic cells
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from iPSC-derived macrophage studies.

claim: Human iPSC-derived macrophages from patients had a modest decrease in uptake of apoptotic cells compared to familial and isogenic controls.
source: and had a modest decrease in uptake of apoptotic cells, in comparison to familial and isogenic controls.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from iPSC-derived macrophage studies.

claim: ACK1 and BRK kinase activity are dispensable for the phagocytosis of polystyrene beads, opsonized cells, and microbes.
source: In contrast, ACK1 and BRK kinase activity are dispensable for the phagocytosis of polystyrene beads, opsonized cells, and microbes.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from phagocytosis assays.

claim: A defective efferocytic response to apoptotic cells may contribute to the auto-immune phenotype of the patients.
source: and that a defective efferocytic response to apoptotic cells may contribute to the auto-immune phenotype of the patients.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: In Family 1, compound heterozygous missense variants in ACK1 (K161Q and A156T) were identified.
source: In Family 1, we identified compound heterozygous missense variants in the non-receptor tyrosine kinase (NRTK) ACK1, which were confirmed by Sanger sequencing (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole exome sequencing and Sanger confirmation, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The two patients in Family 1 were males and developed class IV lupus nephritis between age 10 and 15.
source: The two patients were males and developed a class IV lupus nephritis between age 10 and 15.
evidence: This is clinical data from the patients.

claim: In Family 1, the K161Q allele was inherited from one parent and the A156T allele from the other.
source: The K161Q allele was inherited from one parent and the A156T allele from the other (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is genetic segregation data shown in the pedigree in Figure 1A.

claim: Family 1 has South Asian ancestry, with the closest 1,000 Genomes Project individuals being those from North India (India, Bangladesh, and Pakistan).
source: Principal components analysis (PCA) based on the whole-exome sequencing to analyze population structure, parental inbreeding, and familial linkage (Belkadi et al., 2016) reveals South Asian ancestry, the closest 1,000 Genomes Project individuals being those from North India (India, Bangladesh, and Pakistan, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on PCA analysis of WES data.

claim: The ACK1 mutant alleles A156T and K161Q have not been reported in South Asian (31,442 alleles) or other populations from public databases.
source: The ACK1 mutant alleles, A156T and K161Q (transcript ENST00000333602, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), have not been reported in South Asian (31,442 alleles) or other populations from public database (gnomAD, 1000 genomes project) or our own in-house databases of >10,000 exomes of patients with infectious phenotypes.
evidence: This is based on database searches.

claim: The ACK1 variants A156T and K161Q were not found in DNA from 100 individuals from the small southeastern island from which the family originated.
source: Finally, these variants were not found in DNA from 100 individuals from the small southeastern island from which they originated (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on targeted sequencing of a control population.

claim: ACK1 mutant alleles A156T and K161Q are private to Family 1 and their segregation is compatible with an autosomal recessive trait with complete penetrance.
source: Altogether, ACK1 mutant alleles, A156T and K161Q are private to this family and their segregation is compatible with an autosomal recessive trait with complete penetrance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic data and pedigree analysis.

claim: In Family 2, compound heterozygous missense variants in BRK (G257A and G321R) were identified in three siblings.
source: In Family 2, we identified compound heterozygous missense variants in another NRTK, BRK in three siblings (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from whole exome sequencing, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In Family 2, two patients developed lupus nephritis and the third patient developed severe panniculitis, between the ages of 20 and 30 years.
source: Two patients developed lupus nephritis, and the third patient developed a severe panniculitis, between the ages of 20 and 30 years.
evidence: This is clinical data from the patients.

claim: In Family 2, two patients were female and one male.
source: Two patients were female and one male.
evidence: This is demographic data from the patients.

claim: In Family 2, one parent probably transmitted the G321R allele to their children, and the 2 other parents (who are also siblings) transmitted the G257A allele.
source: One parent, who was not genotyped, probably transmitted the G321R to their children, and the 2 other parents (who are also siblings) transmitted the G257A allele (only one parent was available for genotyping; Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is genetic segregation data inferred from the pedigree and available genotyping.

claim: In Family 2, an unaffected sibling (2.III.2) carries the G321R allele but not the G257A allele.
source: An unaffected sibling (2.III.2) carries the G321R allele but not the G257A allele (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is genetic data from the unaffected sibling shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Family 2 has Sub-Saharan African ancestry, with the closest populations of 1000 genomes project being African Caribbean in Barbados and African Ancestry in Southwest US and Luhya in Webuye in Kenya.
source: PCA analysis showed that individuals from family 2 have Sub-Saharan African ancestry, with the closest populations of 1000 genomes project being African Caribbean in Barbados and African Ancestry in Southwest US and Luhya in Webuye in Kenya (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on PCA analysis of WES data.

claim: The BRK G257A allele is reported with a maximum MAF of approximately 8×10^-5 in Sub-Saharan African subpopulations.
source: These 2 BRK mutant alleles, G257A and G321R are reported with a maximum MAF of ~8×10–5 and 5×10–3 respectively in Sub-Saharan African subpopulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is based on database searches shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The BRK G321R allele is reported with a maximum MAF of approximately 5×10^-3 in Sub-Saharan African subpopulations.
source: These 2 BRK mutant alleles, G257A and G321R are reported with a maximum MAF of ~8×10–5 and 5×10–3 respectively in Sub-Saharan African subpopulations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is based on database searches shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The BRK G257A and G321R alleles predict a homozygosity frequency of approximately 10^-8 and 10^-6, respectively.
source: predicting a homozygosity frequency of ~10–8 and 10–6, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the MAF data.

claim: The BRK alleles are extremely rare outside Africa in the non-African gnomAD populations.
source: These alleles are extremely rare outside Africa in the non-African gnomAD populations.
evidence: This is based on database searches.

claim: The BRK allele frequencies are fully consistent under a recessive model with the overall prevalence of SLE (40–200 per 100,000 individuals).
source: These results are fully consistent under a recessive model with the overall prevalence of SLE (40–200 per 100,000 individuals).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing predicted homozygosity frequency with SLE prevalence.

claim: The ACK1 K161Q, A156T and BRK G257A and G321R variants are all localized in the evolutionarily conserved kinase domains of the two proteins.
source: The ACK1 K161Q A156T and BRK G257A and G321R variants are all localized in the evolutionarily conserved kinase domains of the two proteins (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is shown in the domain architecture and sequence alignment in Figure 1C.

claim: The ACK1 and BRK variants are within the N-terminal (ATP-binding) lobes of the kinase catalytic domains.
source: within the N-terminal (ATP-binding) lobes of the kinase catalytic domains (Lougheed et al., 2004; Thakur et al., 2017; Figure 1D)
evidence: This is shown in the 3D structures in Figure 1D and supported by citations.

claim: The ACK1 and BRK variants are near the positions of other mutations that decrease kinase activity.
source: and near the positions of other mutations that decrease kinase activity (Prieto-Echagüe et al., 2010b; Tsui and Miller, 2015; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on comparison with known mutations and supported by citations.

claim: The ACK1 and BRK variants are all predicted to be deleterious based on CADD corrected with MSC.
source: The variants are all predicted to be deleterious based on combined annotation dependent depletion (CADD) corrected with mutation significance cutoffs (MSC; Kircher et al., 2014; Itan et al., 2016; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction tools shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACK1 A156T is a kinase-dead mutant in vitro.
source: In vitro kinase assays indicated that ACK1 A156T and BRK G321R are kinase-dead mutants, and that ACK1 K161Q and BRK G257A are severe hypomorphs with an ~20% residual kinase activity in vitro (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: BRK G321R is a kinase-dead mutant in vitro.
source: In vitro kinase assays indicated that ACK1 A156T and BRK G321R are kinase-dead mutants, and that ACK1 K161Q and BRK G257A are severe hypomorphs with an ~20% residual kinase activity in vitro (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ACK1 K161Q is a severe hypomorph with approximately 20% residual kinase activity in vitro.
source: In vitro kinase assays indicated that ACK1 A156T and BRK G321R are kinase-dead mutants, and that ACK1 K161Q and BRK G257A are severe hypomorphs with an ~20% residual kinase activity in vitro (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: BRK G257A is a severe hypomorph with approximately 20% residual kinase activity in vitro.
source: In vitro kinase assays indicated that ACK1 A156T and BRK G321R are kinase-dead mutants, and that ACK1 K161Q and BRK G257A are severe hypomorphs with an ~20% residual kinase activity in vitro (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ACK1 A156T and K161Q variants lack auto-phosphorylation activity.
source: ACK1 A156T and K161Q and BRK G321R variants also lacked auto-phosphorylation activity (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: BRK G321R variant lacks auto-phosphorylation activity.
source: ACK1 A156T and K161Q and BRK G321R variants also lacked auto-phosphorylation activity (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ACK1 A156T and K161Q phenocopy the effect of the specific ACK1 kinase inhibitor AIM100.
source: phenocopying the effect of the specific ACK1 and BRK kinase inhibitors AIM100 (Mahajan et al., 2012) and Cpd4f (Oelze et al., 2015) respectively (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: BRK G321R phenocopies the effect of the specific BRK kinase inhibitor Cpd4f.
source: phenocopying the effect of the specific ACK1 and BRK kinase inhibitors AIM100 (Mahajan et al., 2012) and Cpd4f (Oelze et al., 2015) respectively (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: BRK G257A has a small residual auto-phosphorylation activity.
source: while the BRK G257A allele has a small residual activity (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: iPSCs were generated from patient 1-III-1 (ACK1 mutant), his heterozygous parent 1-II-3, patient 2-III-3 (BRK mutant) and her heterozygous sibling 2-III-2.
source: To examine the effects of the mutations in the patient's cells, we generated iPSCs from unrelated WT donors, patient 1-III-1 (ACK1 mutant), his heterozygous parent 1-II-3, patient 2-III-3 (BRK mutant) and her heterozygous sibling 2-III-2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D)
evidence: This describes the generation of iPSC lines shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: hiPSC-derived macrophages from unrelated donors, familial controls, and patients presented with normal morphology, survival, and phenotype.
source: hiPSC-derived macrophages from unrelated donors, familial controls, and patients presented with a normal morphology, survival, and phenotype and expressed comparable amount of ACK1 and BRK at the transcript and protein level (Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2D, 2E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: hiPSC-derived macrophages from unrelated donors, familial controls, and patients expressed comparable amounts of ACK1 and BRK at the transcript and protein level.
source: hiPSC-derived macrophages from unrelated donors, familial controls, and patients presented with a normal morphology, survival, and phenotype and expressed comparable amount of ACK1 and BRK at the transcript and protein level (Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2D, 2E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: ACK1K161Q/A156T macrophages show loss of ACK1 kinase activity in comparison to controls.
source: but an in vitro kinase assay indicated a loss of ACK1 kinase activity in ACK1K161Q/A156T macrophages in comparison to controls (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 2E.

claim: BRKG257A/G321R macrophages show reduced BRK Tyr342 phosphorylation in comparison to controls.
source: We therefore studied BRK kinase activity by IP-WB, which showed reduced BRK Tyr342 phosphorylation in BRKG257A/G321R macrophages in comparison to controls (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from IP-Western blot shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The patients' ACK1 A156T and BRK G321R variants are kinase-dead alleles.
source: These data altogether indicate that the patients' ACK1 A156T and BRK G321R variants are kinase-dead alleles and K161Q and BRK G257A are severe hypomorphs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the biochemical assays.

claim: The patients' ACK1 K161Q and BRK G257A variants are severe hypomorphs.
source: These data altogether indicate that the patients' ACK1 A156T and BRK G321R variants are kinase-dead alleles and K161Q and BRK G257A are severe hypomorphs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the biochemical assays.

claim: Mice that received ACK1 or BRK inhibitors without pristane developed a large array of circulating anti-nuclear IgG antibodies.
source: In the absence of pristane, mice that received ACK1 or BRK inhibitors developed a large array of circulating anti-nuclear IgG antibodies, including but not limited to autoantibodies associated with SLE such as anti-histones, anti-chromatin, anti U1-snRNP, anti-SSA, and anti-Ku (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from mouse studies shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ACK1 and BRK inhibition are sufficient to promote autoimmunity in mice.
source: These data suggested that ACK1 and BRK inhibition are sufficient to promote autoimmunity in mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the autoantibody data from mice.

claim: No glomerular deposit of IgG was observed at 12 weeks in mice that received ACK1 or BRK inhibitors without pristane.
source: We did not observe glomerular deposit of IgG at 12 weeks in these mice (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3B, 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: BALB/cByJ mice which received pristane treatment in addition to ACK1 or BRK inhibitors had increased kidney glomerular deposits of IgG.
source: In contrast, BALB/cByJ mice which received pristane treatment (Satoh and Reeves, 1994) in addition to either ACK1 or BRK inhibitors had increased kidney glomerular deposits of IgG as well as increased serum autoantibody levels including anti-Ku (p70/p80), LA/SSB, Ro-SSA, Histone H4 and H2B, in comparison to DMSO vehicle controls (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from mouse studies shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: BALB/cByJ mice which received pristane treatment in addition to ACK1 or BRK inhibitors had increased serum autoantibody levels including anti-Ku (p70/p80), LA/SSB, Ro-SSA, Histone H4 and H2B.
source: In contrast, BALB/cByJ mice which received pristane treatment (Satoh and Reeves, 1994) in addition to either ACK1 or BRK inhibitors had increased kidney glomerular deposits of IgG as well as increased serum autoantibody levels including anti-Ku (p70/p80), LA/SSB, Ro-SSA, Histone H4 and H2B, in comparison to DMSO vehicle controls (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from mouse studies shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibition of ACK1 or BRK increases serum autoantibody titers and worsens pristane-induced Lupus in WT BALB/cByJ mice.
source: Therefore, inhibition of ACK1 or BRK increase serum autoantibody titers and worsen pristane-induced Lupus in WT BALB/cByJ mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mouse experimental data.

claim: Autosomal recessive ACK1 and BRK kinase deficiency may underlie or contribute to the development of SLE in children and young adults depending on genetic and environmental context.
source: Together with the above genetic analysis, these findings support the hypothesis that autosomal recessive ACK1 and BRK kinase deficiency may underlie or contribute to the development of SLE in children and young adults depending on genetic and environmental context.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the combined genetic and mouse experimental data.

claim: The reference ACK1 and BRK alleles phosphorylate AKT and STAT3, but the patient's ACK1 and BRK variant alleles do not.
source: We found that, in contrast to the reference ACK1 and BRK alleles, the patient's ACK1 and BRK variant alleles do not phosphorylate AKT and STAT3 (Figure 4A and B)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: The reference ACK1 and BRK alleles activate RAC1 to generate RAC-GTP, but the patient's ACK1 and BRK variant alleles do not.
source: and do not activate RAC1 to generate RAC-GTP (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from RAC activation assay shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ACK1 is a downstream target of MERTK.
source: NRTKs such as ACK1 (Mahajan et al., 2005) and PTK2/FAK (Wu et al., 2005) are also downstream targets of the TAM family receptor MERTK
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PTK2/FAK is a downstream target of MERTK.
source: NRTKs such as ACK1 (Mahajan et al., 2005) and PTK2/FAK (Wu et al., 2005) are also downstream targets of the TAM family receptor MERTK
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MERTK is expressed on macrophages and controls the anti-inflammatory engulfment of apoptotic cells.
source: which is expressed on macrophages and controls the anti-inflammatory engulfment of apoptotic cells, a process known as efferocytosis (Scott et al., 2001; Henson and Bratton, 2013; Henson, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MERTK function supported by citations.

claim: Efferocytosis allows for the clearance of apoptotic cells before they undergo necrosis and release intracellular inflammatory molecules.
source: Efferocytosis allows for the clearance of apoptotic cells before they undergo necrosis and release intracellular inflammatory molecules, and simultaneously leads to increased production of anti-inflammatory molecules (TGFβ, IL-10, and PGE2) and a decreased secretion of proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1β, IL-6; Scott et al., 2001; Henson and Bratton, 2013; Henson, 2017; deCathelineau and Henson, 2003; Nagata, 2018; Fadok et al., 1998; Voll et al., 1997; Rothlin et al., 2015; Cvetanovic and Ucker, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about efferocytosis supported by multiple citations.

claim: Efferocytosis leads to increased production of anti-inflammatory molecules (TGFβ, IL-10, and PGE2) and decreased secretion of proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1β, IL-6).
source: Efferocytosis allows for the clearance of apoptotic cells before they undergo necrosis and release intracellular inflammatory molecules, and simultaneously leads to increased production of anti-inflammatory molecules (TGFβ, IL-10, and PGE2) and a decreased secretion of proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1β, IL-6; Scott et al., 2001; Henson and Bratton, 2013; Henson, 2017; deCathelineau and Henson, 2003; Nagata, 2018; Fadok et al., 1998; Voll et al., 1997; Rothlin et al., 2015; Cvetanovic and Ucker, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about efferocytosis supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mice deficient in MFG-E8, MERTK, TIM4, and C1q develop phenotypes associated with autoimmunity.
source: In line with these findings, mice deficient in molecular components used by macrophages to efficiently perform efferocytosis, such as MFG-E8, MERTK, TIM4, and C1q, develop phenotypes associated with autoimmunity (Scott et al., 2001; Cohen et al., 2002; Henson and Bratton, 2013; Nagata, 2018; Fadok et al., 1998; Voll et al., 1997; Cvetanovic and Ucker, 2004; Hanayama et al., 2004; Miyanishi et al., 2012; Colonna et al., 2016; Nagata et al., 2010; Kimani et al., 2014; Hanayama et al., 2002; Kawano and Nagata, 2018; Watanabe-Fukunaga et al., 1992; Singer et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge from mouse models supported by multiple citations.

claim: Defects in efferocytosis are observed in patients with SLE and glomerulonephritis.
source: Furthermore, defects in efferocytosis are also observed in patients with SLE and glomerulonephritis (Nagata, 2018; Herrmann, 1998; Baumann, 2002; Schrijvers et al., 2005; Morioka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SLE pathogenesis supported by citations.

claim: MERTK activated the kinase activity of wild-type ACK1 but not of the ACK1 A156T and ACK1 K161Q variant alleles.
source: In IP kinase assays, MERTK activated the kinase activity of wild-type ACK1 (Mahajan et al., 2005) but not of the ACK1 A156T and ACK1 K161Q variant alleles (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from IP kinase assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: MERTK activated BRK kinase activity.
source: In addition, MERTK also activated BRK kinase activity, but the BRK G321R and G257A alleles were kinase dead and hypomorph variants, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from IP kinase assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The BRK G321R allele is kinase dead in response to MERTK activation.
source: In addition, MERTK also activated BRK kinase activity, but the BRK G321R and G257A alleles were kinase dead and hypomorph variants, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from IP kinase assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The BRK G257A allele is a hypomorph variant in response to MERTK activation.
source: In addition, MERTK also activated BRK kinase activity, but the BRK G321R and G257A alleles were kinase dead and hypomorph variants, respectively (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from IP kinase assays shown in Figure 4D.

claim: MERTK-mediated recognition of PtdSer on apoptotic cells leads to their engulfment, which involves activation of RAC1 for actin reorganization and formation of a phagocytic cup.
source: MERTK mediates recognition of PtdSer on apoptotic cells via GAS6 and Protein S (Scott et al., 2001; Seitz et al., 2007; Cohen et al., 2002) leading to their engulfment, which involves activation of RAC1 for actin reorganization and the formation of a phagocytic cup (Wu et al., 2005; Mao and Finnemann, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MERTK signaling supported by citations.

claim: PtdSer recognition stimulates an anti-inflammatory process mediated in part via AKT and STAT3 and their target genes such as SOCS3.
source: PtdSer recognition also typically stimulates an anti-inflammatory process mediated in part via AKT (Sen et al., 2007) and STAT3 and their target genes such as SOCS3 (Yi et al., 2009; Vergadi et al., 2017; Byles et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2011; Roberts et al., 2017; Matsukawa et al., 2005; Sica and Mantovani, 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge about efferocytosis signaling supported by multiple citations.

claim: PtdSer recognition results in the inhibition of LPS-mediated production of inflammatory mediators such as TNF and IL1β, and the production of cytokines such as IL-10, TGFβ.
source: and results in the inhibition of LPS-mediated production of inflammatory mediators such as TNF and IL1β, and the production of cytokines such as IL-10, TGFβ (Henson and Bratton, 2013; Fadok et al., 1998; Voll et al., 1997; Rothlin et al., 2015; Cvetanovic and Ucker, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about efferocytosis supported by citations.

claim: One consequence of the defective activity of ACK1 and BRK kinase variants might be an impaired efferocytic response to PtdSer on apoptotic cells.
source: Altogether, these data raised the hypothesis that one of the consequences of the defective activity of ACK1 and BRK kinase variants might be an impaired efferocytic response to PtdSer on apoptotic cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the biochemical data.

claim: Macrophages are the main contributors to efferocytosis.
source: Efferocytosis can be carried out by multiple cell types; however, macrophages are the main contributors in this process (Roberts et al., 2017; Parnaik et al., 2000; Nishi et al., 2014; Lazarov et al., 2023).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MERTK kinase activity mediates efferocytosis by human iPSC-derived macrophages.
source: MERTK kinase activity mediates efferocytosis by human iPSC-derived macrophages (Wanke et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: ACK1- and BRK-deficient macrophages, as well as WT macrophages treated with ACK1 or BRK inhibitors, failed to upregulate gene sets associated with AKT signaling and the negative regulation of the inflammatory response.
source: GSEA analysis of differentially expressed genes indicated that, in contrast to control, ACK1- and BRK-deficient macrophages, as well as WT macrophages treated with ACK1 or BRK inhibitors failed to upregulate gene sets associated with AKT signaling and the negative regulation of the inflammatory response (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ATF3, TGIF1, NFIL3, KLF4, SOCS3, DUSP5, CEBPD, and ID3 are among the top-ten genes which expression is induced by apoptotic cells in WT macrophages.
source: Transcriptional repressors including the AKT targets ATF3, TGIF1, NFIL3, and KLF4, the STAT3 targets SOCS3 and DUSP5, as well as CEBPD and the inhibitor of E-BOX DNA Binding ID3 were among the top-ten genes which expression is induced by apoptotic cells in WT macrophages (Figure 4F)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The regulation of ATF3, TGIF1, NFIL3, KLF4, SOCS3, DUSP5, CEBPD, and ID3 by apoptotic cells was lost in mutant and inhibitor-treated macrophages.
source: but this regulation was lost in mutant and inhibitor-treated macrophages (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: ATF3, TGIF1, NFIL3, and KLF4 are involved in the negative regulation of inflammation in macrophages.
source: ATF3, TGIF1, NFIL3, and KLF4 are involved in the negative regulation of inflammation in macrophages (Vergadi et al., 2017; Byles et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2011; Roberts et al., 2017)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: SOCS3 is an inhibitor of the macrophage inflammatory response.
source: SOCS3 is an inhibitor of the macrophage inflammatory response and DUSP5 is a negative regulator of ERK activation (Matsukawa et al., 2005; Sica and Mantovani, 2012; Seo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DUSP5 is a negative regulator of ERK activation.
source: SOCS3 is an inhibitor of the macrophage inflammatory response and DUSP5 is a negative regulator of ERK activation (Matsukawa et al., 2005; Sica and Mantovani, 2012; Seo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The kinase domain of ACK1 and BRK contribute to the macrophage anti-inflammatory gene expression program driven by apoptotic cells.
source: These data suggest that the kinase domain of ACK1 and BRK contribute to the macrophage anti-inflammatory gene expression program driven by apoptotic cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data.

claim: Decreased TNF gene expression by macrophages in response to apoptotic cells was prevented by the ACK1 inhibitor.
source: Decreased TNF gene expression by macrophages in response to apoptotic cells was prevented by the ACK1 inhibitor (Figure 4G)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 4G.

claim: MERTK-deficient mice are susceptible to LPS-induced endotoxic shock.
source: MERTK-deficient mice are susceptible to LPS-induced endotoxic shock (Camenisch et al., 1999)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MERTK-dependent anti-inflammatory program elicited by apoptotic cells on macrophages is evidenced by the reduction of LPS-mediated production of inflammatory mediators such as TNF or IL1β.
source: and MERTK-dependent anti-inflammatory program elicited by apoptotic cells on macrophages is best evidenced by the reduction of LPS-mediated production of inflammatory mediators such as TNF or IL1β (Fadok et al., 1998; Voll et al., 1997; Cvetanovic and Ucker, 2004; Sen et al., 2007; Camenisch et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Isogenic variants and control macrophages produced similar amounts of TNF in response to LPS.
source: Both isogenic variants and control macrophages produced similar amounts of TNF in response to LPS (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from ELISA shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Exposure to apoptotic cells inhibited TNF production in control macrophages by 50% but did not inhibit TNF production in ACK1 and BRK-deficient macrophages.
source: However, exposure to apoptotic cells inhibited TNF production in control macrophages by 50% but did not inhibit TNF production in ACK1 and BRK-deficient macrophages (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from ELISA shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Isogenic variants and control macrophages produced similar amounts of IL1β in response to LPS.
source: Similarly, isogenic variants and control macrophages produced similar amounts of IL1β in response to LPS (Figure 4I)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from ELISA shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Apoptotic cells decreased IL1β production by isogenic macrophages but not by mutant macrophages.
source: but apoptotic cells only decreased IL1β production by isogenic macrophages and not by mutant macrophages (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from ELISA shown in Figure 4I.

claim: ACK1 and BRK kinase activities contribute to the macrophage anti-inflammatory response during efferocytosis.
source: These data altogether indicate that ACK1 and BRK kinase activities contribute to the macrophage anti-inflammatory response during efferocytosis and are required for the decrease of TNF and IL1β production induced by LPS in response to apoptotic cells, a hallmark of their anti-inflammatory effect on macrophages (Henson and Bratton, 2013; Fadok et al., 1998; Voll et al., 1997; Cvetanovic and Ucker, 2004).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ELISA data.

claim: ACK1 and BRK kinase activities are required for the decrease of TNF and IL1β production induced by LPS in response to apoptotic cells.
source: These data altogether indicate that ACK1 and BRK kinase activities contribute to the macrophage anti-inflammatory response during efferocytosis and are required for the decrease of TNF and IL1β production induced by LPS in response to apoptotic cells, a hallmark of their anti-inflammatory effect on macrophages (Henson and Bratton, 2013; Fadok et al., 1998; Voll et al., 1997; Cvetanovic and Ucker, 2004).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ELISA data.

claim: MERTK-dependent signaling for anti-inflammatory response and for cargo engulfment driven by recognition of PtdSer on apoptotic cells are distinct and separable molecular events.
source: MERTK-dependent signaling for anti-inflammatory response and for cargo engulfment driven by recognition of PtdSer on apoptotic cells are distinct and separable molecular events (Tibrewal et al., 2008; Elliott and Ravichandran, 2010)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: RAC1 controls engulfment of apoptotic cells.
source: however because RAC1, which controls engulfment of apoptotic cells (Albert et al., 2000), is a target of ACK1 and BRK (see Figure 4C) as well as PTK2/FAK (Wu et al., 2005)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Isogenic ACK1 and BRK mutant macrophages presented with an altered actin-ring in frustrated engulfment assays.
source: Wild-type iPSC-derived macrophages formed a typical actin-ring; however, isogenic ACK1 and BRK mutant macrophages presented with an altered actin-ring (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Isogenic ACK1 and BRK mutant macrophages had a reduced actin clearance factor.
source: and a reduced actin clearance factor (Figure 5B), indicating an impairment of actin remodeling following binding to PtdSer.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from TIRF microscopy quantification shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The actin-ring was altered and actin clearance factor was decreased in WT macrophages treated with ACK1 and BRK inhibitors.
source: The actin-ring was also altered and actin clearance factor was decreased in WT macrophages treated with ACK1 and BRK inhibitors in comparison to controls (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from TIRF microscopy shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The kinase activity of ACK1 and BRK contributes to link PtdSer receptors to cytoskeleton rearrangement at the phagocytic synapse.
source: These data suggest the kinase activity of ACK1 and BRK contributes to link PtdSer receptors to cytoskeleton rearrangement at the phagocytic synapse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TIRF microscopy data.

claim: Engulfment of apoptotic thymocytes was moderately reduced by 10-20% in ACK1 and BRK isogenic mutant macrophages.
source: We found that engulfment of apoptotic thymocytes labeled with the pH-sensitive probe pHrodo (Nishi et al., 2014; Miksa et al., 2009; Shiraishi et al., 2004) was only moderately reduced, by 10–20% in ACK1 and BRK isogenic mutant macrophages (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from flow cytometry shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A 30-min exposure of WT macrophages to ACK1 inhibitors AIM100 and R-9b, and BRK inhibitor Cpd4f reproduced the modest reduction in engulfment of apoptotic cells.
source: This phenotype, although modest, was reproducible by a 30-min exposure of WT macrophages to two different ACK1 inhibitors, AIM100 (2 µM) and R-9b (Lawrence et al., 2015; 4µM), and to the BRK inhibitor Cpd4f (0.5 μM; Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from flow cytometry shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ACK1 and BRK genetic kinase deficiency or inhibitors did not prevent Fc-dependent phagocytosis of opsonized red blood cells.
source: This reduced uptake of apoptotic cells was not attributable to a global engulfment defect, because ACK1 and BRK genetic kinase deficiency or inhibitors did not prevent Fc-dependent phagocytosis of a large cargo such as opsonized red blood cells (Figure 5G)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from flow cytometry shown in Figure 5G.

claim: ACK1 and BRK genetic kinase deficiency or inhibitors did not prevent the uptake of polystyrene beads.
source: or the uptake of polystyrene beads (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from flow cytometry shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ACK1 and BRK genetic kinase deficiency or inhibitors did not prevent the uptake of microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi.
source: or microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from flow cytometry shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: The kinase activity of ACK1 and BRK participate to the formation of phagocytic synapse but are largely dispensable for engulfment of apoptotic cells.
source: Altogether, these data show that the kinase activity of ACK1 and BRK participate to the formation of phagocytic synapse but are largely dispensable for engulfment of apoptotic cells and are not required for phagocytosis of microbes and opsonized cargo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phagocytosis assay data.

claim: The kinase activity of ACK1 and BRK are not required for phagocytosis of microbes and opsonized cargo.
source: Altogether, these data show that the kinase activity of ACK1 and BRK participate to the formation of phagocytic synapse but are largely dispensable for engulfment of apoptotic cells and are not required for phagocytosis of microbes and opsonized cargo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phagocytosis assay data.

claim: Analysis of 27 GWAS studies of SLE found no common variants in the close vicinity of the ACK1 (TNK2) or BRK (PTK6) genes with a p-value lower than 5×10^-8.
source: However, we analyzed 27 GWAS studies of SLE (https://www.gwascentral.org/), and none of them reported a common variant within close genetic distance of the TNK2/ACK1 or PTK6/BRK genes with a p-value lower than 5x10–8, a statistical threshold of genome-wide significance for GWAS.
evidence: This is based on analysis of published GWAS data.

claim: ACK1 and BRK deficiency are likely to only account for the genetic basis of SLE in a minority of patients.
source: ACK1 and BRK deficiency are thus likely to only account for the genetic basis of SLE in a minority of patients.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GWAS analysis and rarity of the variants.

claim: Autosomal recessive TNK2/ACK1 and PTK6/BRK kinase deficiency probably underlie the development of SLE in a small proportion of children and young adults.
source: Altogether, the present data indicate that autosomal recessive TNK2/ACK1 and PTK6/BRK kinase deficiency probably underlie the development of SLE in a small proportion of children and young adults, depending on genetic and environmental context.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on all the genetic and experimental data.

claim: TNK2/ACK1 and PTK6/BRK kinase deficiencies impair the MERTK-dependent anti-inflammatory response of the patients' macrophages to apoptotic cells during efferocytosis.
source: Our results also suggest that TNK2/ACK1 and PTK6/BRK kinase deficiencies, in addition to dysregulating B and T cell survival and activation (Kasprzycka et al., 2006; Sridaran et al., 2022), also impair the MERTK-dependent anti-inflammatory response of the patients' macrophages to apoptotic cells during efferocytosis, and to a lesser extent the engulfment of the apoptotic cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the macrophage functional studies.

claim: TNK2/ACK1 and PTK6/BRK kinase deficiencies impair the engulfment of apoptotic cells to a lesser extent than the anti-inflammatory response.
source: Our results also suggest that TNK2/ACK1 and PTK6/BRK kinase deficiencies, in addition to dysregulating B and T cell survival and activation (Kasprzycka et al., 2006; Sridaran et al., 2022), also impair the MERTK-dependent anti-inflammatory response of the patients' macrophages to apoptotic cells during efferocytosis, and to a lesser extent the engulfment of the apoptotic cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the macrophage functional studies.

claim: The NRTK PTK2/FAK and Src are important for MERTK-dependent engulfment of apoptotic cells.
source: The NRTK PTK2/FAK and Src are important for the former (Tibrewal et al., 2008; Tao et al., 2015)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PTK2/FAK is dispensable for the MERTK-dependent anti-inflammatory response.
source: while PTK2/FAK is dispensable for the latter (Tibrewal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TNK2/ACK1 and PTK6/BRK are more important for the control of TNF and IL1β production than for engulfment itself.
source: Our experiments suggest that in contrast, TNK2/ACK1 and PTK6/BRK are more important for the control of TNF and IL1β production than for engulfment itself.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional studies comparing anti-inflammatory response and engulfment.

claim: The study identifies a rare Mendelian cause of severe SLE.
source: Altogether, our observations identify a rare Mendelian cause of severe SLE and a role for the NRTK TNK2/ACK1 and PTK6/BRK in efferocytosis, thereby contributing to a molecular and cellular dissection of SLE.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The study identifies a role for the NRTK TNK2/ACK1 and PTK6/BRK in efferocytosis.
source: Altogether, our observations identify a rare Mendelian cause of severe SLE and a role for the NRTK TNK2/ACK1 and PTK6/BRK in efferocytosis, thereby contributing to a molecular and cellular dissection of SLE.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
